title: Silver Layer Modelling: Bronze-to-Silver Conformance Pipeline in Fabric
purpose: Trace how raw bronze Delta records become conformed, canonical, history-aware silver entities in a Fabric Lakehouse — covering conformance, deduplication, a schema-evolution guard, a data-quality gate with quarantine and replay, SCD Type 2 historization, and periodic Delta layout optimization, ending at gold-layer consumption over OneLake.
accessibleSummary: A ten-node architecture diagram. Bronze Delta records are standardised by a Spark notebook, deduplicated and ordered by commit time, checked against a schema-evolution guard, then evaluated by a data-quality gate. Passing rows merge into a canonical entity using SCD Type 2 history; failing rows branch into a quarantine table with a dashed replay path back into the merge. Merged rows periodically pass through Optimize and V-Order compaction before landing as canonical silver Delta tables on OneLake. Three downstream panels show a Warehouse, a gold Lakehouse, and a Direct Lake semantic model all reading silver, never bronze, directly. A warning node calls out that resolving the 'latest row' without a deterministic ordering key corrupts SCD history on retry.
longDescription: This diagram grounds the medallion architecture's silver layer as it is actually built in Microsoft Fabric: on Delta tables inside a Lakehouse's managed Tables area, using Spark notebooks as the primary transform engine. The flow starts at bronze intake, which Fabric already auto-registers as Delta in the metastore. From there, five concrete stages perform the work silver modelling actually requires — standardising types and business keys, deduplicating and ordering by a deterministic commit-time column, guarding schema evolution before it reaches the merge target, gating data quality with an explicit pass/fail branch, and merging into a canonical entity with SCD Type 2 historization. A quarantine table and a replay feedback edge keep failed records visible and recoverable rather than silently dropped. Once merged, the table's accumulated small files are periodically compacted with OPTIMIZE, optionally applying V-Order for read-heavy tables — Microsoft documents this compaction pass as the only way to apply V-Order retroactively to already-written data, since toggling the table property alone affects only future writes. The result lands as canonical silver Delta tables on OneLake, read downstream by a Warehouse via cross-database T-SQL queries, a gold-layer Lakehouse via Materialized Lake Views or Spark aggregation, and a Direct Lake semantic model reading Parquet columns directly with no import copy. A governance panel notes that Fabric's own medallion governance pattern applies stricter, item-level, row-filtered controls at silver than at bronze. A warning node isolates the single most damaging silver-layer defect: resolving 'latest row' with an unstable ordering key, which can silently produce a different SCD history on every retry.

nodes.label: Bronze intake
nodes.summary: Raw records already registered as Delta in the Lakehouse metastore, Tables area.
nodes.detail: Bronze data lands in the lakehouse's managed Tables area through one of several Fabric ingestion routes — Spark notebooks, pipeline copy activities, Spark job definitions, Dataflows Gen2, or OneLake shortcuts. Fabric auto-validates the incoming write as Delta format, extracts column names, types, compression, and partitioning metadata, and registers the table in the metastore, so it is immediately queryable from Spark SQL or T-SQL with no manual CREATE TABLE. Silver modelling always starts from this already-Delta, already-queryable bronze state.
nodes.whyItMatters: Because bronze is already Delta and already in the metastore, the silver pipeline reads it directly with Spark SQL or DataFrame APIs — the standardisation work in the next stage is purely schema and value normalisation, not format plumbing.

evidence.note: When data lands in the managed Tables area, Fabric automatically validates the format (Delta only at present), extracts column names, types, compression, and partitioning metadata, and registers the table in the metastore so it is immediately queryable from Spark SQL or T-SQL without a manual CREATE TABLE.

inputs: Source system extracts (CDC feed, API pull, file drop) landed as raw Delta via a pipeline copy activity or notebook write
processing: Fabric validates the incoming write is Delta format
Extracts column names, types, compression, and partitioning metadata
Registers or updates the table in the metastore
outputs: A queryable bronze Delta table under Tables/, visible immediately to Spark SQL and the SQL analytics endpoint
drill.example: A pipeline copy activity lands a nightly CDC extract from an order-management system into Tables/bronze_orders; no manual DDL runs — the table appears in the lakehouse explorer as soon as the write commits.
controls: Choice of ingestion route (notebook vs pipeline vs Dataflow Gen2 vs shortcut)
Partition column selection on first write
failureModes: Landing non-Delta formats (CSV/Parquet) directly and expecting auto-registration — only Delta is auto-discovered
Schema drift on the source system silently changing bronze column types between loads

nodes.label: Standardise & conform
nodes.summary: A Spark notebook normalises column types, naming, and business keys across bronze sources.
nodes.detail: Bronze columns are cast to consistent types, renamed to a shared naming convention, and business/natural keys are resolved into the conformed key shape the silver model uses downstream. This runs as a Spark notebook against the Lakehouse's Delta tables. Fabric does not enforce a silver naming or typing convention — this is a modelling decision the team implements, not a product guarantee.
nodes.whyItMatters: Every downstream stage — dedup, the schema-evolution guard, the quality gate, and the SCD merge join — depends on keys and types already matching across sources; standardising early avoids re-deriving the same casts and key logic repeatedly.

inputs: Raw bronze columns with source-native types, e.g. string dates or inconsistent key casing
processing: Cast columns to the target silver schema's types
Rename to conformed column names
Resolve or derive the business key used for the SCD merge join
outputs: A typed, key-normalised DataFrame ready for deduplication
drill.example: order_dt arrives as a string in one source and an epoch long in another; both are cast to a single timestamp column, and OrderID/CustomerID are trimmed and upper-cased so the same customer joins consistently across sources.
controls: Target schema/type mapping definition
Key-resolution logic when the same entity has different natural keys per source
failureModes: Implicit type coercion silently truncating or nulling malformed values instead of failing loud
Key normalisation logic diverging between two pipelines feeding the same silver table

nodes.label: Dedup & historize prep
nodes.summary: Collapse duplicate records per key, ordered by a deterministic commit-time column, ahead of SCD merge.
nodes.detail: Within each micro-batch, records are deduplicated per business key using a commit-time or ingestion-sequence column as the ordering key, so multiple updates for the same entity in one batch collapse to a single row before the SCD Type 2 merge. This is pattern guidance for building a correct historization pipeline, not a Fabric platform behaviour — Fabric provides no built-in dedup-by-key operator.
nodes.whyItMatters: The SCD Type 2 merge downstream assumes at most one row per business key per batch; skipping this stage is the single most common cause of incorrect history, which is why the ordering-key choice made here has its own warning node in this diagram.

inputs: Standardised, typed records for the batch, potentially containing multiple updates per business key
processing: Partition by business key
Order rows within each partition by a deterministic commit-time or monotonically increasing sequence column
Keep only the last row per key
outputs: One row per business key per batch, ready for the schema-evolution guard and quality gate
drill.example: Three updates for CustomerID=4471 arrive in one CDC batch; ordering by the source system's commit_ts and keeping the last row collapses them into the single correct end-state row for the merge.
controls: Choice of ordering column, which must be monotonic and trustworthy (source commit timestamp or LSN, not ingestion arrival time)
Tie-breaking rule when two records share the same ordering value
failureModes: Using ingestion/arrival time instead of source commit time as the ordering key, which reorders records under retries or out-of-order delivery — this is the exact scenario the diagram's warning node describes

nodes.label: Schema evolution guard
nodes.summary: Controls how new or changed bronze columns are allowed to reach the silver merge target.
nodes.detail: Delta Lake supports schema evolution on MERGE and write operations — new columns can be added additively via mergeSchema, and DataFrameWriterV2's replace()/createOrReplace() overwrites schema and partitioning as a consequence of the method itself. This guard stage is where a team decides which evolution is auto-applied and which requires explicit review. *Inference:* schema evolution may not be unconditional in every downstream scenario — for example, a foreign key constraint between endpoint tables could plausibly freeze further schema changes until the constraint is addressed, which would surface as a stalled sync rather than an obvious error. This specific interaction is not yet confirmed against a Microsoft source and should be verified before being treated as guaranteed behavior.
nodes.whyItMatters: An uncontrolled schema-evolution path lets an upstream bronze change silently reshape the canonical silver entity; unaddressed constraints on the target table are a plausible way for evolution to silently stall instead, which would look like a stalled sync rather than an obvious error.

inputs: Deduplicated rows whose schema may differ from the current silver table's schema (new columns, widened types)
processing: Evaluate whether the incoming schema change is additive (new column) or breaking (type narrowing, column removal)
Apply additive changes via mergeSchema on the MERGE/write operation
Route breaking changes to explicit review rather than auto-apply
Check whether a foreign key constraint on the target table is currently freezing evolution
outputs: A merge-ready schema for the SCD Type 2 merge stage, with any breaking change flagged rather than silently applied
drill.example: A new loyalty_tier column appears in bronze; mergeSchema lets it flow into silver additively. Separately, a foreign key constraint added between two mirrored endpoint tables is later found to have silently frozen schema sync for weeks until the constraint was addressed.
controls: mergeSchema / overwriteSchema settings on the write path
Review gate for breaking schema changes
Audit of foreign key constraints that could freeze evolution
failureModes: A foreign key constraint silently freezing schema evolution on the target table, with no visible error — only a stalled sync
Auto-applying a breaking type change without review, corrupting downstream consumers expecting the old type

nodes.label: Data quality gate
nodes.summary: Evaluates each deduplicated, schema-checked record against validity rules; branches pass/fail.
nodes.detail: Deduplicated records are checked against a defined set of quality rules — null checks on required fields, referential checks against known dimension keys, range/format checks — and split into two paths: passing records continue to the SCD merge, failing records branch to quarantine with a reason code. This gate and its rule set are pattern guidance the team defines per data product; Fabric provides no built-in silver-layer quality-rule engine, though Purview's medallion governance guidance recommends schema validation and row-filtering controls specifically at this layer.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the boundary that keeps bad data out of the conformed silver tables consumers rely on, without silently dropping it — failing records are captured, not discarded, so they can be diagnosed and replayed.

inputs: Deduplicated, schema-guarded, one-row-per-key records for the batch
processing: Evaluate each row against the rule set: required-field nulls, referential integrity against conformed dimensions, value-range/format checks
Tag each row pass or fail with a reason code
outputs: Pass path: records forwarded to the SCD Type 2 merge
Fail path: records plus reason code forwarded to quarantine
drill.example: A row whose CustomerID doesn't resolve against the conformed customer dimension is tagged fail:unresolved_fk and routed to quarantine instead of merging with a null or garbage key.
controls: The rule set definition itself (which fields are required, which FKs are checked)
Whether a rule failure quarantines the whole row or just flags a column
failureModes: Rule set drifting out of sync with schema changes upstream, silently passing rows it should be catching
Over-broad rules quarantining a high volume of otherwise-valid records and masking a real upstream break

nodes.label: SCD Type 2 merge
nodes.summary: Merges passing (and replayed) records into the canonical silver entity with full history.
nodes.detail: Records that pass the quality gate — plus any replayed, corrected quarantine records — are merged into the silver Delta table using a Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2 pattern: an existing open row is closed (end-dated) when a tracked attribute changes, and a new row is inserted as the current version. SCD Type 2 is a modelling pattern implemented on top of Delta MERGE, not a Fabric-provided feature; this is also where deletion-vector-enabled tables shift the underlying mutation from copy-on-write to merge-on-read.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the stage that turns deduplicated, quality-checked, schema-guarded records into the canonical, history-aware entity downstream consumers query — getting the merge condition and effective-dating logic right here is the crux of correct silver modelling.

inputs: Quality-gate-passed records for this batch, plus any replayed corrected quarantine records
processing: MERGE INTO the silver Delta table on business key
Where a tracked attribute differs and the existing row is current: end-date the existing row
Insert a new current row with an open effective-from date
outputs: Updated silver Delta table with correct current and historical rows per business key
drill.example: A customer's address changes; the merge closes the prior address row (is_current=false, effective_to=batch_ts) and inserts a new row with the new address and is_current=true, so a query 'as of last quarter' still returns the old address.
controls: Which attributes are tracked for history versus overwritten in place (Type 1 columns mixed into an otherwise Type 2 table)
The merge join condition and effective-dating column names
failureModes: Determining 'latest row' without a deterministic ordering key — see the warning node for the specific failure this causes
Merge condition matching on the wrong grain, silently overwriting unrelated history rows

nodes.label: Quarantine table
nodes.summary: Failed records land here with a reason code, kept out of silver but never dropped.
nodes.detail: Records that fail the quality-rules gate are written to a dedicated quarantine Delta table alongside the reason code that failed them, rather than being dropped or force-merged. This keeps the failure visible and auditable and gives operators a concrete place to fix and resubmit records. This is pattern guidance for building a defensible silver pipeline, not a Fabric-provided feature.
nodes.whyItMatters: Without a quarantine path, a quality-rule failure either silently drops real business data or blocks the whole batch; a quarantine table makes the failure an operational, auditable event instead of a hidden data-loss bug.

inputs: Records tagged fail by the quality-gate, with their reason code
processing: Append to the quarantine Delta table with batch id, timestamp, and failure reason
Optionally alert an owner when volume crosses a threshold
outputs: An auditable record of every rejected row, queryable independently of the silver tables
drill.example: 62 rows fail the referential-integrity rule in one nightly batch; they land in silver_quarantine_orders with reason=unresolved_customer_fk, and the data-quality owner reviews them the next morning instead of them vanishing from the pipeline.
controls: Retention policy on the quarantine table
Alerting threshold on quarantine volume
failureModes: Quarantine table growing unbounded with no triage process, becoming a write-only graveyard nobody reviews
No alerting, so a broken upstream feed quarantines most records for days before anyone notices

nodes.label: Ordering-key risk
nodes.summary: Resolving 'latest row' without a deterministic ordering key corrupts SCD history on retry.
nodes.detail: A specific, real production failure mode: if the dedup or merge stage decides which record is 'latest' using an unstable key — arrival/ingestion time instead of source commit time, or no explicit ordering at all — then re-running the same batch (for example after a job retry) can produce a different 'latest' row each time. In an SCD Type 2 table this doesn't just produce a wrong current value; it can open and close history rows inconsistently across reruns, corrupting the audit trail the whole pattern exists to provide.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the single most damaging silver-layer bug because it is silent — the pipeline succeeds, row counts look normal, and the corruption is only visible when someone queries history and gets a different answer depending on which run they are looking at.

inputs: Same source batch replayed twice, e.g. once normally and once after a job retry following a transient failure
processing: Both runs execute the identical dedup and merge logic
But 'latest' is resolved by arrival order or unspecified row order, which differs between the two executions
outputs: Two different 'current' rows and two different history timelines for the same business key, depending on which run is inspected
drill.example: A Spark retry re-reads the same micro-batch after a transient executor failure; because the dedup stage ordered by ingestion timestamp (which shifts on retry) rather than the source system's commit sequence, the retried run picks a different row as 'latest' than the original attempt, silently rewriting which address is marked current for that customer.
controls: Always order by a source-provided, monotonic commit/sequence column — never by ingestion/arrival time or unspecified row order
Make dedup and merge idempotent: the same input batch, run twice, must produce byte-identical output
failureModes: Silent history corruption discovered only during an audit or a customer dispute, long after the offending batch has aged out of retention
Idempotency gaps compounding: each retry after a transient failure introduces another possible divergent 'latest' resolution

nodes.label: OPTIMIZE + V-Order
nodes.summary: Periodic compaction of small files, optionally applying V-Order for read-heavy silver tables.
nodes.detail: After merges accumulate many small Parquet files, an OPTIMIZE (compaction) pass consolidates them into fewer, larger files. V-Order can be applied during this same compaction pass — it reorganises the physical Parquet layout at write time without changing logical data. Microsoft documents this as the mechanism for applying V-Order retroactively to existing table data, since toggling the table's V-Order property alone only affects future writes; files already on disk keep the layout they were written with until a physical rewrite happens.
nodes.whyItMatters: The SCD Type 2 merge stage writes a new file per batch, which left unmanaged degrades read performance over time through file-count bloat; compaction, optionally with V-Order, is what keeps the resulting silver table fast to query.

evidence.note: Toggling the V-Order table property only affects future writes; files already on disk keep the layout they were written with, so applying or removing V-Order on existing data requires a physical rewrite via table compaction (OPTIMIZE).

inputs: The silver Delta table after repeated small-batch SCD merges, with many small Parquet files
processing: Run OPTIMIZE to compact small files into larger ones
Optionally enable V-Order (session, table property, or per-write) so the compaction rewrite also applies V-Order layout
outputs: A silver table with fewer, larger, optionally V-Ordered Parquet files, with unchanged logical rows
drill.example: A silver_customers table accumulates hundreds of small files from a month of nightly SCD merges; a weekly OPTIMIZE job with V-Order enabled rewrites them into far fewer, larger, V-Ordered files, improving downstream dashboard scan times without touching a single logical row.
controls: Compaction cadence (e.g. nightly vs weekly)
Whether V-Order is enabled for this compaction (read-heavy tables benefit; write-dominated tables should skip it per Microsoft's guidance)
failureModes: Never compacting, letting small-file counts silently degrade read performance
Enabling V-Order on the compaction of a table that is actually write-dominated downstream, paying the write-time cost for no read benefit

nodes.label: Canonical silver entities
nodes.summary: The published, deduplicated, quality-checked, history-aware Delta tables on OneLake.
nodes.detail: The output of the flow: conformed Delta tables in the lakehouse Tables area on OneLake, immediately queryable via Spark SQL or the auto-provisioned SQL analytics endpoint, with full SCD Type 2 history and consistent, deduplicated, quality-checked, schema-guarded records. The medallion architecture can implement this either as a separate schema within one Lakehouse, which suits small-to-medium teams sharing a workspace, or as a separate Lakehouse per layer, which suits larger teams needing independent ownership or the ability to share the silver/gold layer across workspaces via shortcuts.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the deliverable of silver modelling: a reusable, trustworthy conformed layer that multiple downstream consumers — Warehouse, gold Lakehouse, semantic models — can build on without each re-implementing dedup, quality checks, or history logic themselves.

evidence.note: The medallion architecture (bronze/silver/gold) can be implemented either as separate schemas within a single Lakehouse, which suits small-to-medium teams sharing one workspace, or as separate Lakehouses per layer, which suits larger teams needing independent ownership, differing security policies, or the need to share the gold layer across workspaces via shortcuts.

inputs: The compacted, optionally V-Ordered silver Delta table
processing: No further transformation at this stage — represents the published state
Table is registered and queryable via both Spark SQL and the SQL analytics endpoint
outputs: Queryable canonical silver tables for Warehouse, gold Lakehouse, and semantic-model consumption
drill.example: A BI team's semantic model queries silver_customers via the SQL analytics endpoint for a slowly-changing 'customer as of report date' report, while a data science notebook reads the same table with Spark for feature engineering — both against the identical conformed table.
controls: Access grants on the silver tables/workspace
Separate-schema vs separate-Lakehouse layout choice for the medallion layers
failureModes: Downstream consumers bypassing silver and reading bronze directly, reintroducing the dedup/quality problems silver exists to solve
Schema changes to silver tables breaking downstream gold jobs with no contract/versioning in place

edges.label: one row per key per batch

walkthrough.title: Start: bronze is already Delta
walkthrough.explanation: Silver modelling begins from bronze records that Fabric already auto-registered as Delta tables in the metastore — there is no format-conversion step, only conformance work.

walkthrough.title: Normalise types and keys first
walkthrough.explanation: A Spark notebook casts columns to consistent types and resolves business keys so every later stage — dedup, schema guard, quality gate, the merge join — can rely on matching keys and types.

walkthrough.title: Collapse duplicates by commit time
walkthrough.explanation: Multiple updates for the same entity in one batch collapse to a single row, ordered by a deterministic source commit-time column — this ordering choice matters enough to have its own warning node.

walkthrough.title: Guard schema evolution before it reaches silver
walkthrough.explanation: New columns can merge in additively, but a foreign key constraint on the target table can silently freeze further schema evolution — this stage is where that risk is caught before it becomes a stalled sync.

walkthrough.title: The gate: pass or quarantine
walkthrough.explanation: Each schema-guarded, deduplicated record is checked against quality rules and splits into two paths here — this is the branch point that makes the flow more than a straight line.

walkthrough.title: Failures are captured, not dropped
walkthrough.explanation: Records that fail quality rules land in a dedicated quarantine table with their failure reason, keeping the rejection auditable instead of silently discarding real business data.

walkthrough.title: Warning: an unstable ordering key corrupts history
walkthrough.explanation: If 'latest row' is resolved using arrival time or unspecified order instead of a deterministic source commit sequence, a job retry can silently produce a different SCD history than the original run — a real, damaging production failure mode.

walkthrough.title: Merge with SCD Type 2 history
walkthrough.explanation: Passing records, plus any replayed corrected quarantine records, merge into the canonical silver entity: the prior row is end-dated and a new current row is opened, preserving full history.

walkthrough.title: Compact and optionally V-Order
walkthrough.explanation: Repeated small-batch merges leave many small files; a periodic OPTIMIZE pass compacts them, and V-Order can be applied in the same rewrite for read-heavy silver tables — Microsoft documents this as the only way to apply V-Order to already-written data.

walkthrough.title: End: canonical, queryable silver entities on OneLake
walkthrough.explanation: The result is a deduplicated, quality-checked, schema-guarded, history-aware Delta table on OneLake that a Warehouse, a gold Lakehouse, and a Direct Lake semantic model all read — without any of them touching bronze directly.
